Observationes — The observation archive of Tycho Brahe, and the printed catalogue of stars

The 38 manuscript volumes in which Tycho Brahe’s observations survive — where each is, what it contains, in whose hand, what it was copied from, how it descended, and on which pages of Dreyer’s edition it is printed — with the catalogue of 777 fixed stars he printed from the record in 1602, star by star, and the new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 as he tabled them.

1Introduction

The record of Tycho Brahe's observing survives in 38 manuscript volumes. Seventeen are at the Royal Danish Library in Copenhagen: eight original nightly protocols (Dreyer's Codices B–I), two books of comet observations, a working volume of theory and observations, Elias Olai's quadrant book of 1589, four contemporary transcripts (Codices A, K, L and P) and Erasmus Bartholin's compilation of the 1660s. Twenty are at the Austrian National Library in Vienna: the nineteen annual fair copies, arranged by subject, that Tycho had made from the protocols (Dreyer's Codex V), and a working catalogue of 296 zodiacal stars. One octavo of the earliest observations is lost. J. L. E. Dreyer printed the whole record as volumes X–XIII of the Opera Omnia (1923–26), and this chapter indexes those printed pages back to the codices they were set from.

From the record Tycho printed one thing directly: the catalogue of 777 fixed stars for the year 1600, in the Progymnasmata of 1602 — given here star by star in his own coordinates, with the modern identification of each and the distance between his place and ours. The new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 are given as they stand in these books and as he printed their result.

How to read an entry

The catalogue (§2) is one row per codex and sorts on any column; the register (§3) gives each codex in full, in the order of Dreyer's letters, with his description of the hand quoted, the scribe attribution and its basis, what the volume was copied from, the pages of the Opera Omnia set from it, the library's catalogue record and, where one exists, the facsimile. Every codex keeps a stable key printed in its record; a link of the form ?volume=O_GKS311 opens the page at that record. A star of the catalogue is cited by its number in the 1602 print (st-307 is Polaris), a page of the printed edition by volume and page (p-XI-394).

Two grades are used and kept apart. The record grade (A–D) states how securely a volume's identity, extent and dates are established: A for every extant codex here, B for the lost octavo. The hand grade (B–D) on the fair copies and transcripts states how securely the engrossing scribe is identified by the documentary prior — who was on Hven in that year — and not by palaeography: B one primary candidate, C several, D unattributed or the one named candidate excluded by date. A star's identification grade (1–6) is Verbunt & van Gent's: 1 secure and the nearest modern star, 2 secure though not the nearest, 3 probable, 4 possible, 5 not identified, 6 a double entry.

How this chapter was made

The codices are described from Dreyer's Prolegomena editoris to Opera Omnia X (pp. I–XXVII), read in the Latin and in an English working translation made for this chapter, against the two libraries' own catalogue records and the leaf counts of the Vienna Tabulae codicum (1873). The pages of the printed edition are assigned to their codices by Dreyer's stated rule (p. XXV) and the volumes' tables of contents; the page-by-page summaries of §5 come from a reading of 976 of the 1,850 pages of volumes X–XIII made in 2026 from copies of the print, an irregular sample that omits pp. 1–18 of vol. X, and the other pages are indexed only by volume and year.

The star catalogue is founded on the keyed text of the three editions published by Verbunt & van Gent (2010) from Dreyer's reprint, in which the 777 stars of the 1602 print are selected by their sequence number and the readings peculiar to 1602 are restored from their variant table; each star carries their Hipparcos identification and its grade. A reading of the same catalogue made in 2026 from a copy of the 1602 print (759 rows) is collated against that text star by star and its verdict recorded: 647 readings agree, 19 differ in a detail, 44 were misread by more than three minutes of arc, 12 were filed under the wrong constellation, 37 could be placed against no star, and 55 stars of the print — Ursa Minor entire among them — were never read. The accuracy figures of §6 are computed twice: by this chapter's own method (nearest neighbour in the Yale Bright Star Catalogue within 40′ of Tycho's place rotated to the modern frame) and from Verbunt & van Gent's graded identifications. The nova's and the comet's figures are read from the page images of Opera Omnia II and IV; the readings made earlier from copies of the 1602 and 1588 prints are kept beside them as witnesses.

Facsimiles were probed on 5 September 2026: the Austrian National Library's catalogue records no digital copy of any of its twenty volumes; the Royal Danish Library's records show none for fifteen of its seventeen, and the two known viewers resolve.

What the figures are not

The count of codices is Dreyer's list plus his second Vienna codex and the two Copenhagen volumes he did not letter; it is not a count of everything at the two libraries that carries Tycho's astronomy (§11). The genre of a codex states what it is, its institution where it is, and its originality its relation to the observing; a "protocol" is an original nightly record, and only eight survive. The hand grade measures who could have written a fair copy, not who did. No page of the printed edition is called autograph here: Codex G, from which vol. XIII pp. 1–115 are set, is a scribal codex in which Dreyer sets Tycho's own entries in italic type. The star count is the print's, not the archive's: no star of §6 is joined to a page of §5, because the catalogue is Tycho's reduction of many nights and the print does not say which. The accuracy medians are over the stars named beside each figure and, for this chapter's method, still mix Tycho's error with the identification's. The page index is a sample of the printed edition until the remaining pages are read; every count in §5 states its denominator.

What this chapter does not contain

The 1,004 stars of the 1598 manuscript catalogue are not tabled; its witnesses are named in §6 and the text is Opera Omnia III pp. 333–373. The reductions made from the observations — Tycho's own theories, Kepler's Rudolphine Tables (1627), Curtz's Historia Coelestis (1666) — belong to the afterlife told in Receptio. The weather diary kept on Hven beside the observations is Diarium's. The texts of De nova stella and the farewell elegy in Codex G are read in Scripta; their figures and the codex stay here. The hand of Tycho himself is the Graphonomicon's subject; this chapter bridges to its specimens and does not repeat them.

3Register of the codices

The codices in full, in the order of Dreyer's letters — the Copenhagen codices A to P (J is not used), then the two Copenhagen volumes he did not letter and the lost octavo, then the nineteen Vienna fair copies year by year and the Vienna working catalogue. Each record quotes Dreyer's statement on the hand from the Prolegomena with his page, gives the library's own title, the leaf counts with their unit, the scribe attribution with its grade and basis, what the volume was copied from and what was copied from it, the printed pages set from it with their page images, the catalogue record, the facsimile or the absence of one, and the bridges to the persons in Familia, the specimens in the Graphonomicon, the episodes in Receptio and the open questions.

The live KB catalogue title (soeg.kb.dk; Ilsøe, Støbeskeen 1999, p. 582) reads 'Tychonis Brahei Fasciculus Observationum Solis et Planetarum, subjuncto calculo Planetarum ex observationibus annorum 1599 et 1600', in the same hand (possibly Longomontanus) as GKS 1827, whereas Dreyer, Opera Omnia X, identifies A. Coll. Reg. 1829 as his 'Codex L'. The two descriptions are irreconcilable as one volume; neighbours GKS 1827/1828/1830 align Dreyer↔KB with no offset, so a post-Dreyer rebinding/renumbering is the likely cause. The volume is recorded here per the live KB catalogue. No other candidate is found in the Royal Library's catalogue, and the catalogue title dates only the appended calculation, not the main observations.

4Concordance

Dreyer's letters are the join that holds the archive together: each Copenhagen archetype of 1582–1601 has its Vienna fair copies, made year by year from it, and the transcripts and comet books have their exemplars. The table gives, per letter, the shelfmark, the volumes copied from it and the pages of the Opera Omnia set from it; the bands below show the same join as Dreyer's own picture of it — one original, the fair copies drawn from it — with the year 1593, whose fair copy was lost before Kepler's death, marked where it should stand. A concordance to Curtz's Historia Coelestis (1666) does not yet exist (§11).

The archetypes and their fair copies

5The printed edition, page by page

Dreyer printed the observations in volumes X–XIII of the Opera Omnia, year by year, each year in the subject order of the fair copies — Sun, Moon, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, fixed stars — with the comets of 1577–1596 at the end of vol. XIII and the indices in vol. XV. The table below gives each volume's years, printed extent, the codices it was set from and its page images at the Internet Archive. The register that follows is one row per page that the 2026 reading reached, by volume and year: its printed page linked to the page image, the body observed, the codex it was set from and the reading's summary of the page. 976 of the 1,850 pages of volumes X–XIII are here, and 55 pages of apparatus; the rows are a sample, and every filter states its count against the whole. The rows that carry no body are pages of reductions, tables or mixed entries.

6The catalogue of stars

6.1 The witnesses

The catalogue of fixed stars for the year 1600 exists in three editions: the manuscript of 1598 with 1,004 stars, presented in fine copies to patrons; the shorter version of 777 stars that Tycho printed in the Progymnasmata of 1602 (pp. 303–332), omitting the constellation Centaurus and the additional stars at the end of many constellations; and Kepler's printing of the full 1,004 in the Rudolphine Tables of 1627. The table in §6.2 is the 1602 print, star by star, in the text established by Verbunt & van Gent (2010) from Dreyer's reprint (Opera Omnia II pp. 258–280), with each star's identification in the Hipparcos catalogue and its grade, the offset between Tycho's place and the modern one, the page of the 1915 reprint on which it stands, and the verdict of the collation against the 2026 reading of the print. The archive's own working catalogues — the 723 stars at the end of Codex G and the 296 zodiacal stars of Cod. 10709, both printed at the end of vol. XI — and the manuscript witnesses of the 1598 catalogue are listed first.

Presentation apograph of the 1004-star restitution; main catalogue only (26 ll.). Its dedication recipient is unrecorded — blank in both Dreyer's TBOO III manuscript list (p. 411) and Truffa's 2002 census; resolving it needs inspection of the dedication leaf in Vienna.		catalogue record
Cod. 10707Vienna, Austrian National Library1600Star-catalogue restitution 1600 — Corraduz copy, w/ unique Appendix
Presentation apograph of the 1004-star restitution, dedicated by Tycho's autograph inscription (March 1600) to Rudolf Corraduz (Corraducius), Imperial Vice-Chancellor: 'Illustri & Generoso Domino RVDOLPHO CORADVCIO … Imperii Procancellario … ddt Tycho Brahe Anno 1600 Mense Martio' (TBOO III, p. 417). It is the longest of the three (31 against 26 leaves) because it alone carries the Stellarum inerrantium Restitutionis Appendix — a popularising supplement giving 36 star-positions adapted to Emperor Rudolf II's nativity , which Dreyer first printed from this codex alone (TBOO III, pp. 379–389: 'Invenitur autem appendix in uno … codice Vindobonensi lat. 10707'). 		catalogue record

The printed editions: the surviving copies of the 1602 Progymnasmata; the Uraniborg sheets of 1592; the printed editions. The text of record for the table below is Verbunt & van Gent's keyed edition (CDS J/A+A/516/A28), collated against the reprint in Opera Omnia II pp. 258–280, the pages of which are linked from every row.

6.2 The 777 stars of the 1602 print

Emendation of the text of record. the table numbers K 469–482 as 1602 stars 527–539, gives the manuscript's Com 2 (K 470) the number 540 — Ophiuchus 1's — and the duplicate Com 15 (K 483) none, so 540 occurs twice and 526 not at all — TBOO II p. 273: Coma has 14 stars in the print, opening with 'In cuspide primi & borealis trianguli' (K 469) and closing with 'Quae est in australi cuspide △ parui' (K 483); Ophiuchus opens with 'In capite' (K 328) immediately after. Emended here: K 469 → 526, K 471–482 → 527–538, K 483 → 539, K 470 → not in the print.

6.3 The 2026 reading collated against the print

A reading of the 1602 catalogue was made in 2026 by machine from the page scans of a copy of the print in a private collection (759 rows). It is kept as a witness and collated here against the text of record, by the rule: same constellation after the twelve moves; first the nearest place within 3′ (one to one), then a reading still unjoined to the nearest unjoined star of its constellation within 60′ — a misread row; beyond 60′ the row has no counterpart.

VerdictRows
agrees647
differs in a detail19
misread (more than 3′ off)44
read under the wrong constellation12
rows placed against no star of their constellation37
stars of the print not read55

Of the 55 stars of the print the reading never reached, 7 are Ursa Minor entire — the reading stopped at the foot of one page and resumed at the head of the next — and the rest fall at page boundaries and binding gutters; none is southern. The twelve rows read under the wrong constellation are ten stars of Pisces filed under Andromeda and Triangulum and two informes of Bootes filed under Draco; the page image of TBOO II p. 266 settles them.

6.4 The sky as Tycho tabled it

6.5 Accuracy

Two measures are given. This chapter's measure rotates each of Tycho's places (equinox and ecliptic of 1600) to the modern equatorial frame with the full precession matrix and finds the nearest star of the Yale Bright Star Catalogue within 40′; the separation is his error, and the residual is the same after the catalogue's median zero-point offset is removed. Verbunt & van Gent's measure is the offset between Tycho's place and their graded Hipparcos identification, over the stars they identify securely or probably. The two agree: a median of about three minutes of arc over the whole catalogue, with the brightest stars better and a tail of gross errors — about one star in nine beyond ten minutes — that Verbunt & van Gent attribute to computing and copying, not observing. Every median below prints the number of stars it is taken over.

Ptolemy's places scatter by about 25′ and Ulugh Beg's (1437) by about 20′ against the modern sky (Verbunt & van Gent 2012 (A&A 544, A31)). This chapter's method: Tycho's ecliptic places (equinox & ecliptic of 1600) are rotated to J2000 equatorial via the full IAU-1976 precession matrix and the 1600 obliquity, then nearest-neighbour matched to the modern bright-star sky (within 40′); the separation is his positional error. Residual scatter is the error after removing the catalogue's median zero-point offset (Δλ·cosβ = +1.21′, Δβ = +0.75′). The modern reference is the Yale Bright Star Catalogue, 5th ed. (1991); the graded identifications are Verbunt & van Gent, 'Three editions of the star catalogue of Tycho Brahe' (2010); the earlier assessments are Dreyer (1916), Wesley, 'The accuracy of Tycho Brahe's instruments' (1978) on the instruments and Rawlins, 'Tycho's 1004-star catalog' (1993) on the catalogue.

7The new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577

7.1 The new star of 1572

Tycho measured the new star’s distances from the chief stars of Cassiopeia with the sextant; they showed no daily parallax, and he placed the star among the fixed stars.

“Longitudinem eius, satis praecise disposuerimus, si eam in part. 6. ′.54 ♉ absolute constitutam fuisse, pronunciauerimus, Latitudine quoque partium 53. ′.45 existente”

The reading made in 2026 from a copy of the print in a private collection gave the latitude as 54°35′; longitude agrees (6°54′ ♉); latitude read as 54°35′ where the print gives 53°45′ — the comparison tables on p. 369 (the star's place by Copernican and Alfonsine star places, 54°05′ and 54°0′) are the likely source of the misread; declination 61°47′ agrees.

Brightness and colour

Tycho set down a month-by-month decline (Progymnasmata, p. 301). In November 1572 the star equalled Venus in size; through December it nearly rivalled Jupiter; in January 1573 it was a little less than Jupiter but still brighter than the first-magnitude stars. By February and March it was of the first magnitude, by April and May of the second, and through the summer it sank to the third — the size of the larger stars of Cassiopeia. By October it was of the fourth order, by the end of that year and into January barely above the fifth, in February 1574 of the sixth and smallest sort; and in March 1574 it grew so faint that it ceased altogether to be seen. Its colour changed as it faded. At its brightest, when it equalled Venus and Jupiter, it shone with a whitish (albicanti), clear and pleasant light; and Tycho affirms (p. 466) that it varied its colour, unlike the constancy of the other stars — which he takes as further proof that it belonged to the celestial and not the elementary world.

The narrative gives no explicit date of discovery; it begins simply 'In Novembri'. The observation span Tycho gives runs from November 1572, when the star equalled Venus, through to March 1574, when it faded below visibility — about sixteen months of continuous monitoring.

Constitisse autem hanc Peregrinam Stellam toto suae durationis Tempore, in eodem prorsus Caeli loco, instar Affixarum Stellarum... Neque enim vllum proprium motum interea obtinere cognoscebatur, sed solummodo Reuolutioni vniuersali diurnae... obtemperauit.
That this strange star stood, through the whole time of its duration, in exactly the same place of the sky, like the fixed stars... For it was found to have no proper motion of its own, but obeyed only the universal daily revolution. (p. 303)
In Nouembri (uti dixi) Veneris Stella quantitate visebatur. Per Decembrem Iouis Sidus ferme aemulabatur... donec vltimo Mense Martio adeo exilis reddita sit, vt conspici celerius prorsus desineret.
In November, as I said, it appeared the size of the star Venus. Through December it nearly rivalled the star Jupiter... until at last, in the month of March, it became so faint that it presently ceased to be seen at all. (p. 301)
...omnium aperissime ostendebat illam [inter Affixa]rum Stellarum supremam... sedes... delegisse, omniumq; Planetarum gyratio[nes] [&] infimarum elementarium Mundano exuperasse.
...it showed most plainly of all that it had chosen its seat among the highest of the fixed stars, surpassing all the revolutions of the planets and the lowest elementary world. (p. 171, Liber V)
...obseruando videlicet easdem binas Stellas, siue Cassiopeæ, siue alterius Asterismi per vtrumq; Instrumentum, tam Vetus illud, quam Nouum Sextantem nulli Parallaxi obnoxium.
...observing, that is, the same pairs of stars, whether of Cassiopeia or of another asterism, through each instrument — both that old one and the new sextant, which is subject to no parallax. (p. 343). The freedom from parallax here is the sextant's, not the star's: Tycho is comparing his two instruments, having found the older one's star-distances a few minutes too large; the passage does not bear on the star's own parallax.

Bridges: the surviving copies of De nova stella; SN 1572 — Tycho's Supernova and its remnant; The apocalyptic sky — the 1572 nova and 1577 comet read as signs; the pages of the printed record for 1572–1573: vol. XI p. 238, vol. XV p. 46.

The tail

On 16 November Tycho measured the tail: 'Longitudo caudæ 17 Grad. Latitudo 6 Grad. 30 min. vbi erat latissima' — some 17 degrees long, and 6° 30′ across at its widest point. On the later nights the log fixes its endpoints by azimuth and altitude ('Initii caudæ' and 'Finis caudæ' on 30 November; 'Finis caudæ' and a second, doubtfully read 'Rursum caudæ' (?) on 1 December), from which the tail's direction across the sky follows. The leaves read here give only that — length, breadth and endpoints. Tycho's celebrated claim about the direction itself, that the tail pointed away not from the Sun but from Venus (a coincidence he later suspected of being an optical illusion, since a tail averted from the Sun would be the more natural thing), belongs to the argument of De mundi, not to these pages.

Read from a copy of the 1588 print in a private collection; the passage in Opera Omnia IV is not yet located (§11).

Longitudo caudæ 17 Grad. Latitudo 6 Grad. 30 min. vbi erat latissima.
The tail's length 17 degrees, its breadth 6 degrees 30 minutes, where it was widest (observation of 16 Nov 1577).
quod Luna Horizonti vicina, non loco apparebat, in quo reuera erat (prout Optica ratio po[stulat])
...that the Moon, near the horizon, did not appear in the place where it really was (as optical/parallax reasoning requires) — Tycho reasoning about parallactic displacement, the same effect whose near-absence in the comet proved it lay far above the Moon.
Ideòq; longitudo Cometæ in P. 1. M. 17. latitudo P. 27. M. 46.
And thus the comet's longitude is at 1 deg 17 min, latitude 27 deg 46 min (north) — the computed position for 15 December 1577, a representative result of the parallax-triangle method.

Bridges: the autograph comet book, Codex N (GKS 1826); the transcript, Codex P (GKS 1827); the pages of the printed comet observations (vol. XIII pp. 287–304, 41 rows read); the surviving copies of De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis (1588); Tycho's comets recomputed — the 19th-century orbit reductions (1854).

8Hands

Who wrote the volumes is answered at three levels. Dreyer states, codex by codex, how much of each is in Tycho's own hand, and his edition sets those passages in italic; his statements are gathered here with their pages. For the nineteen fair copies and the three Copenhagen transcripts the engrossing hand is not signed, and the attributions below rest on the documentary prior — which assistants were on Hven in the year the volume was copied — not on palaeography; each carries its grade and its basis in words. The one palaeographic apparatus in this portal is the Graphonomicon of Tycho's own hand, whose specimens from five of these codices are linked from the register; no assistant's hand has yet been studied the same way.

Cod. 106681594BChristen Longomontanus—As 1592 — Longomontanus primary, few alternatives (the 1593 volume is lost). Tycho's own hand now rare (Dreyer's 'in posterioribus pauca').
Cod. 106691595BChristen Longomontanus—Longomontanus primary; firmly in Dreyer's rare-Tycho zone (Cod. 10669 onward).
Cod. 106701596C—Christen Longomontanus, Johannes EriksenJohannes Eriksen joins in 1596, creating a genuine two-way split with Longomontanus. Tycho's own hand now rare (Dreyer's 'in posterioribus pauca').
Cod. 106711597C—Christen Longomontanus, Johannes EriksenLongomontanus departs 1 Jun 1597 — the early part of the year is Longomontanus-plausible, the remainder Eriksen. (Tycho appended David Fabricius's autograph observations.)
Cod. 106721598D—Johannes Eriksen, Frans TengnagelAn exile volume: Hven abandoned 1597 (Wandsbek, then Wittenberg). Longomontanus gone; no documented engrossing scribe. Unattributed — Eriksen and Tengnagel are weak, unconfirmed candidates.
Cod. 106731599D—Frans Tengnagel, Johannes EriksenAn exile volume (Wittenberg → Prague/Benátky). No documented engrossing scribe. Unattributed.
Cod. 106741600C—Christen Longomontanus, Johannes Eriksen, Frans TengnagelLongomontanus rejoined Tycho at Prague in 1600 and is again a candidate; Eriksen returning, Tengnagel present. A genuine multi-way split.
Cod. 106751601C—Christen Longomontanus, Johannes Eriksen, Frans TengnagelLongomontanus with Tycho until his death (24 Oct 1601); Johannes Eriksen was Tycho's personal secretary by spring 1601 (Christianson). Both strong candidates; Tengnagel also present.

The method is a documentary prior: which assistants were on Hven, and in what seniority, in the year the volume was copied (Dreyer's roster from a loose sheet of Hans Crol's, 1588/89; the letters). Which apographa are in Longomontanus's hand vs other assistants? is the open question. Hans Crol and Johannes Eriksen have no record in Familia yet and are named without a link.

Tycho's own hand in these codices

Specimens in the Graphonomicon: GKS 1825 kvart: specimen kb-gks-1825; GKS 311 folio: specimen kb-gks-311; GKS 312 folio: specimen kb-gks-312; GKS 316 folio: specimen kb-gks-316; GKS 1826 kvart: specimen kb-gks-1826. The Graphonomicon is the portal's palaeographic apparatus for Tycho's hand; it does not yet cover any assistant's.

9Transmission, 1587–1926

The custody of the books from Tycho's death to Dreyer's edition, as dated events, each with Dreyer's page in the Prolegomena or the source that carries it. The archetypes, which Kepler kept and his son sold to Frederik III in 1655, went to Paris with Rømer in 1672 and came home in 1707; the fair copies, which reached Albert Curtz by a route no one recorded, were printed as the Historia Coelestis in 1666 and remain in Vienna.

11Desiderata

What this chapter does not yet have, does not yet know, or has reason to doubt, with the source that would settle each.

Eighteen stars of the 1602 print never read from the copy of the print

The 2026 reading of the printed catalogue from a copy of the Progymnasmata in a private collection recovered 759 of the 777 stars; the 18 it did not read — Ursa Minor entire, Polaris included, two each in Corona Borealis, Cygnus, Ophiuchus and Hydra, one each in Aquarius, Eridanus and Triangulum — all stand on pages the passes read, at page boundaries and gutters. The catalogue is now founded on Verbunt & van Gent's keyed text and the reading is a collation witness; a second reading of these 18 rows would complete the witness.

Sources: Verbunt & van Gent, 'Three editions of the star catalogue of Tycho Brahe' (2010).

The three Vienna paper bundles (Cod. 10686, 10688, 10689)

Dreyer used three large bundles of letters and papers at Vienna that carry copies of some observations (TBOO XIII p. 98 note: 'Apographum harum observationum in cod. Vindob. lat. 10689 f 26r sqq'). They are not registered here; a leaf-level description would settle which observations they witness.

Sources: Dreyer, Opera Omnia X — Prolegomena (codex descriptions, Codices A–V).

The archive's own star catalogues as tabled records

GKS 316 ff. 164–186 (723 stars) and Cod. 10709 (296 stars near the zodiac, 1589) were printed by Dreyer at the end of TBOO XI (pp. 383–412) and in TBOO III p. 409; the appendices of TBOO XII (pp. 231–265, a catalogue to 1588) and XIII (pp. 61–77, to 1595) print further working catalogues whose manuscript witnesses the Prolegomena do not name. None is tabled star by star here.

Sources: Dreyer, Opera Omnia X — Prolegomena (codex descriptions, Codices A–V), Dreyer (ed.), Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia III (1916).

GKS 1829 as Dreyer's Codex L

Dreyer names 'A. Coll. Reg. 1829' as his Codex L, the 214-leaf transcript of the 1585 observations, and himself explains its tail of 1598–1600 computations; the KB catalogue titles the volume by that tail. The identification is kept as probable pending a leaf count or an image check.

Sources: Dreyer, Opera Omnia X — Prolegomena (codex descriptions, Codices A–V), Royal Danish Library catalogue (soeg.kb.dk), Ilsøe, Det kongelige Bibliotek i støbeskeen (1999).

Dreyer's per-passage hand notes

Dreyer transcribed the marginal notes of Codex A ('in Tycho's hand but written later', 'in Longomontanus's hand again') into the edition and sets Tycho's autograph passages in italic throughout TBOO X–XIII. Harvesting those loci from the footnotes of the four volumes would give the assistants' hands a palaeographic layer the documentary-prior attributions of §8 lack.

Sources: Dreyer, Opera Omnia X — Prolegomena (codex descriptions, Codices A–V).

A concordance to the Historia Coelestis (1666)

Curtz's edition was printed from the Vienna fair copies, without the years before 1582 and without 1593, with signs misread as numerals and pages skipped. A page-by-page concordance from the codices to the 1666 print does not exist; Bartholin's Specimen recognitionis (1668) collates the year 1582 only.

Sources: Dreyer, Opera Omnia X — Prolegomena (codex descriptions, Codices A–V), Bartholin, Specimen recognitionis (1668).

The remaining pages of the printed edition

The page index (§5) rests on a 2026 reading of 976 of the 1,850 pages of TBOO X–XIII, an irregular sample that omits pp. 1–18 of vol. X; the other pages are indexed only by volume and year range. archive.org holds page images and OCR of all four volumes.

Sources: Opera Omnia X–XIII, XV — archive.org facsimiles.

Facsimiles of the thirty-six volumes without one

Two volumes have a public facsimile (GKS 1824, GKS 316). The Austrian National Library's catalogue records no digital copy of any of the nineteen fair copies or of Cod. 10709; the Royal Danish Library's catalogue shows no online link for the other fifteen Copenhagen volumes (probed 5 September 2026). The autograph protocols GKS 311–318 and GKS 1825–1826 are the obvious targets.

Sources: Royal Danish Library catalogue (soeg.kb.dk), Austrian National Library catalogue (search.onb.ac.at).

Hans Crol and Johannes Eriksen in the Familia

Both are candidate scribes of fair copies (Crol to his death on Hven in November 1591; Eriksen from 1596 and Tycho's secretary by 1601) and neither has a record in the Familia chapter, so the attributions naming them cannot link.

Sources: Dreyer, Opera Omnia X — Prolegomena (codex descriptions, Codices A–V).

The Copenhagen leaf counts

For the nineteen Vienna volumes the catalogue's leaf counts agree with Dreyer's to the leaf; for the Copenhagen codices Dreyer's counts and the counts an earlier version of this register carried disagreed on nine of ten, and only GKS 313 has been checked against the KB catalogue (which agrees with Dreyer). The other fourteen KB extents want the same check.

Sources: Dreyer, Opera Omnia X — Prolegomena (codex descriptions, Codices A–V), Royal Danish Library catalogue (soeg.kb.dk).

The lost octavo after 1804

The small octavo of 1563–1574 was in Paris in 1697, returned to Copenhagen in 1707, lent to Christian Hvass about 1778 and reported in France in 1804. Nothing later is known.

Sources: Dreyer, Opera Omnia X — Prolegomena (codex descriptions, Codices A–V).

Related Copenhagen manuscripts outside this register

GKS 320 (the Astronomia hypothetica) and GKS 1832 (planetary tables, possibly in Bartholin's hand) are Tycho-orbit manuscripts at the Royal Library that carry no observations and are not registered here.

Sources: Royal Danish Library catalogue (soeg.kb.dk).

The comet's tail in De mundi

The tail measurements (16 November 1577: 17° long, 6°30′ across at its widest) and Tycho's discussion of the tail's direction are quoted from a copy of the 1588 print in a private collection; their pages in TBOO IV have not yet been located and read.

Sources: Dreyer (ed.), Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia IV (1922).
